NFL Betting Guide: Spreads, Totals, and Key Numbers Explained

Published August 20, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The NFL is the single biggest betting market in the United States, and it plays by a slightly different set of rules than other sports. Football has fewer scoring events than basketball or baseball, and almost all of them come in chunks of 3 (a field goal) or 7 (a touchdown plus extra point). That single fact shapes nearly everything about how NFL lines are built and how sharp bettors think about them. This guide covers the three core bet types — spreads, totals, and moneylines — and the "key numbers" concept that's specific to football.

In this guide

  1. The point spread, and why it's the default NFL bet
  2. Key numbers: why 3 and 7 matter more than any other margin
  3. Totals (over/under) in the NFL
  4. How weather can move a total
  5. Moneyline vs. spread: when each makes more sense

The point spread, and why it's the default NFL bet

A point spread handicaps the favorite so both sides of a game are, in theory, equally attractive to bet. If the Chiefs are favored by 6.5 over the Broncos (written as Chiefs -6.5, Broncos +6.5), a bet on the Chiefs only wins if they win by 7 or more points. A bet on the Broncos wins if they lose by 6 or fewer points, or win outright. The ".5" exists specifically to prevent a push (a tie, where both bets are refunded) — sportsbooks use half-points on the vast majority of NFL spreads for exactly this reason.

Spreads move throughout the week based on where money is coming in and any relevant news (most commonly a starting quarterback's injury status). The number you see on Tuesday is rarely the exact number still posted at kickoff on Sunday.

Key numbers: why 3 and 7 matter more than any other margin

Because touchdowns (7 points with the extra point) and field goals (3 points) account for the large majority of NFL scoring plays, final margins cluster heavily around a small set of numbers — most of all 3, then 7, then smaller clusters at 6, 10, and 14. A spread of 2.5 or 3.5 behaves very differently from a spread of 3 flat, even though the difference looks tiny on paper, because a huge share of NFL games are decided by exactly a field goal.

This is why oddsmakers defend the number 3 more aggressively than any other point in football, and why sharp bettors pay close attention to whether they're getting +3 or +3.5, or laying -3 versus -2.5. Half a point on either side of a key number can be worth meaningfully more than half a point anywhere else on the scale.

Final marginApprox. share of NFL games (illustrative)Why it happens
3 pointsMost common single marginOne team wins by exactly a field goal
7 pointsSecond most commonOne team wins by a touchdown + extra point
6 pointsNotable clusterA touchdown without the extra point, or two field goals vs. one TD
10 & 14 pointsSmaller clustersMultiples of field goals and touchdowns

These figures are illustrative of the pattern, not a live statistical feed — the underlying point is structural (football scores in 3s and 7s) and holds up season after season, which is why "key numbers" is treated as a fundamental concept rather than a passing trend.

Totals (over/under) in the NFL

The total is a bet on the combined score of both teams, regardless of who wins. If the total is set at 44.5, an Over bettor wins if the combined score is 45 or more; an Under bettor wins if it's 44 or fewer. Like spreads, NFL totals cluster around key numbers too — 41, 44, and 47 are common landing points because they sit at natural combinations of field goals and touchdowns from both teams.

Totals move for different reasons than spreads: pace of play, offensive/defensive matchup quality, and expected game script (a blowout tends to see more clock-killing running plays late, which can suppress scoring relative to a close, fast-paced game).

How weather can move a total

Football is one of the few major US sports played outdoors in genuinely adverse conditions, and wind is the single biggest weather factor for bettors to know about — far more than rain or cold on their own. Sustained wind in the mid-teens (mph) or higher tends to suppress passing efficiency and field goal accuracy, which is why a total can drop by a point or more between the open and kickoff if a forecast worsens over the week. Dome and retractable-roof stadiums remove this variable entirely when the roof is closed.

Takeaway: In the NFL specifically, the half-point (or lack of one) around 3 and 7 is worth more attention than in almost any other betting decision you'll make on a football game. Get comfortable checking the exact number, not just the team you like.

Moneyline vs. spread: when each makes more sense

A moneyline bet is simply picking the winner, with no margin attached — you're paid at odds reflecting how big a favorite or underdog a team is. For a close game (a 2- or 3-point spread), the moneyline and spread often carry similar risk profiles, and preference comes down to whether you want spread insurance (win even if the favorite wins by less than the number) versus a cleaner, no-math outcome. For a big mismatch (a 10+ point spread), the favorite's moneyline gets expensive fast, since you're risking a lot to win a little — which is when many bettors shift toward the spread, a smaller alternate spread, or simply pass on the game. See our broader bet types explained guide for how moneylines, spreads, and parlays compare across sports generally.

Frequently asked questions

Why do NFL spreads so often land on 2.5 or 3.5 instead of exactly 3?

The half-point removes the possibility of a push. Since exactly 3 is the single most common margin in football, books use half-points around it specifically to force a winner on one side rather than refunding everyone.

Does the key-number concept apply to the total as well as the spread?

Yes, though less sharply. Totals cluster around numbers reachable by combinations of field goals and touchdowns from both teams (like 41, 44, and 47), so the same "half-point near a key number matters more" logic applies, just spread across more possible numbers.

Is the moneyline ever better value than the spread for a big favorite?

It depends entirely on the odds offered and your own view of the game — there's no universal answer. The tradeoff is structural: the moneyline requires only a win, while the spread requires winning by more than the number, and the price of each reflects that difference.

Why do NFL lines move more in the days right before kickoff?

Injury reports (especially at quarterback), practice participation news, and the bulk of public betting volume are heavily concentrated in the 48 hours before a Sunday game, which is when you'll typically see the fastest line movement.
